q1: False. The viewport meta tag is critical for responsive design. Without it, mobile browsers render pages at a fake desktop width and scale them down, making text tiny.
q2: <meta charset="UTF-8">. This meta tag declares the character encoding for the document, telling the browser how to interpret the text.
q3: <title>. The <title> element sets the browser tab text, bookmark name, and default search-result title.
q4: The site looks zoomed out with tiny text. Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render at a fake desktop width (usually 980px) and scale it down.
q5: To avoid encoding issues and re-parsing. Browsers may re-parse the page if charset is declared too late, potentially causing display issues with non-ASCII characters.
q6: <meta name="description">. This is not required for valid HTML, though it's recommended for SEO. <!DOCTYPE html>, <title>, and <html> are required.
q7: To enable correct mobile rendering. The viewport meta tag prevents mobile browsers from using the fake desktop width and ensures proper scaling.
q8: Virtually all characters and emoji from all languages. UTF-8 is a universal character encoding that covers almost all characters and symbols used worldwide.
q9: <title> sets browser tab text, <h1> is visible on-page heading. They serve different purposes and both should typically exist on a page.
q10: Matches CSS viewport width to the device width. This tells the browser to use the actual device width rather than a fake desktop width for rendering.
